# 1. TRUE or FALSE:
  1) False, bagging approach is used to reduce variance by averaging predictions, that should not lead to overfitting;
  2) False, because odds are related to probability like this: p = odds/ (1+odds), so in our case the probability is p = 0.15/1.15 = 0.13, which is lower, not higher;
  3) False, hierarchical clustering is an unsupervised method for grouping observations, not useful at all for causal questions;
  4) False, since censoring is connected to "not having further mutations" then the mechanism is not independent from radiation, as radiation is what causes the mutations, or lack of them;
  5) False, removing these variables could lead to omitted variable bias.
  
# 2. Choosing correct answers and justifying
 1) d, because out-of-the bag observations are those that are not used to fit a particular bagged tree, which then would follow that error made on this data are errors made on data not in training sample;
 2) b and d, because both of these models manae variance and bias tradeoff with a parameter, which other models here do not do.
 3) e, because PCA is essentially trying to orders components in order of most to least variance explanatory, none of the other options make sense here;
 4) b, c and d, since this is a causal question, causal methods need to be used, others do not play the part;
 5) c, because for grouping items based on their similarity, hierarchical clustering as an unsupervised method is best.

# Problem 2

a) 

```{r 2a}
# I'll recreate the matrix in the task as R object
Matrix <- matrix(c(0, 0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.8, 
                   0.2, 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.1,
                   0.6, 0.3, 0, 0.6, 0.7,

                   0.8, 0.1, 0.7, 0.9, 0), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)

d <- as.dist(Matrix)

# Using complete linkage and plotting the results
hc_linked_comp <- hclust(d, method = "complete")
plot(hc_linked_comp, main = "Complete Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")

heights <- hc_linked_comp$height

# Using single linkage and plotting the results
hc_linked_single <- hclust(d, method = "single")
plot(hc_linked_single, main = "Single Linkage Dendrogram",
     xlab = "Observation", ylab = "Height")
# Again, adding heights
heights_single <- hc_linked_single$height
text(x = 4, y = heights_single[1] + 0.01, labels = heights_single[1], col = "red", cex = 0.9)

text(x = 1.5, y = heights_single[4] - 0.02, labels = heights_single[4], col = "red", cex = 0.9)
```

b) If the data scientist wanted to cut dendrograms into two parts, for complete linkage, one cluster would have 2 and 5, while the other cluster would have 3, 1 and 4. For single linkage one cluster would only consist of observation 4 and the other cluster would feature 3, 1, 2 and 5.
 
c)
 

# Problem 3

a) 

```{r 3a}
# For this task too, I will use R
# First, I will create a points matrix as given in the task

Points <- matrix(c(1, 32,
                   2, 16,
                   4, 8,
                   8, 4,
                   16, 2,
                   32, 1), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

# Calculating distances
distance_euc <- dist(Points, method = "euclidean")
# Creating dendrogram linkages
hc_dist_euc_single <- hclust(distance_euc, method = "single")
hc_dist_euc_complete <- hclust(distance_euc, method = "complete")
hc_dist_euc_average <- hclust(distance_euc, method = "average")

# Plotting them all
plot(hc_dist_euc_single, main = "Single Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
plot(hc_dist_euc_complete, main = "Complete Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
plot(hc_dist_euc_average, main = "Average Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
```

b) To find out for which linkage methods the dendrograms will differ I will use code. But before doing that, my guess is that the dendrograms will be different for all linkage methods because the data scientists dissimilarity function is very different to the Euclidean distance function.
```{r 3b}
# Creating a function to calculate the data scientists dissimilarity function
dissimilarity_function <- function(points) {
  n <- nrow(points)
  matrix <- matrix(0, n, n)
  for (i in 1:(n-1)) {
    for (j in (i+1):n) {
      diff1 <- abs(points[i, 1] - points[j, 1])
      diff2 <- abs(points[i, 2] - points[j, 2])
      matrix[i, j] <- max(diff1, diff2) / min(diff1, diff2)
      matrix[j, i] <- matrix[i, j]
    }
  }
  return(as.dist(matrix))
}

# Calculating distances
distance_scientist <- dissimilarity_function(Points)

# Creating dendrogram linkages
hc_dist_scien_single <- hclust(distance_scientist, method = "single")
hc_dist_scien_complete <- hclust(distance_scientist, method = "complete")
hc_dist_scien_average <- hclust(distance_scientist, method = "average")

# Plotting them all
plot(hc_dist_scien_single, main = "Single Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
plot(hc_dist_scien_complete, main = "Complete Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
plot(hc_dist_scien_average, main = "Average Linkage Dendroram",
     xlab= "Observation", ylab = "Height")
```

Observing the results, I can see that in fact, the dendrograms are different for all linkage methods. Using this distance function it is also the case that complete and average linkage methods produce the same dendrograms, while they were different using the Euclidean distance.
